questions.questionText: A sample of water contains dissolved sodium chloride and a small amount of insoluble sand. Describe a suitable sequence of separation methods and explain the scientific principle used at each stage. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A school laboratory.
questions.explanation: Use filtration first to remove insoluble sand because the solid particles are retained by the filter while the solution passes through. Then use simple distillation to obtain pure water; water is vaporised and condensed while dissolved salt remains in the flask. If the aim is to recover the salt instead, evaporate the water or crystallise the salt solution, using controlled heating.

questions.questionText: An element X has atomic number 13 and mass number 27. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of X, and explain how an ion X3+ forms. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A small-scale water-treatment investigation.
questions.explanation: Protons = 13. Neutrons = 27 − 13 = 14. A neutral atom has 13 electrons. X3+ forms when three electrons are removed, leaving 10 electrons.

questions.questionText: Explain why magnesium oxide has a high melting point and why molten magnesium oxide conducts electricity whereas solid magnesium oxide does not. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: An industrial chemistry exercise.
questions.explanation: MgO has a giant ionic lattice containing strong electrostatic attractions between Mg2+ and O2− ions, requiring much energy to overcome. In the solid the ions are fixed in position and cannot carry charge through the lattice. When molten, the ions are mobile and can carry electrical charge.

questions.questionText: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Calculate the amount, in moles, in 10.0 g of CaCO3 (Mr = 100), then calculate the volume of CO2 at r.t.p. produced if CaCO3 is in excess of acid. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A mining and manufacturing case study.
questions.explanation: Moles of CaCO3 = 10.0/100 = 0.100 mol. The equation gives a 1:1 mole ratio of CaCO3:CO2, so CO2 = 0.100 mol. At r.t.p. 1 mol gas occupies about 24 dm3, so volume = 0.100 × 24 = 2.40 dm3.

questions.questionText: A student reacts equal masses of calcium carbonate with excess hydrochloric acid. Experiment A uses large chips and Experiment B uses powder. Explain which experiment is faster and describe two other changes that could increase the rate. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A household chemistry investigation.
questions.explanation: Powder reacts faster because it exposes a larger surface area, producing more frequent successful collisions. Increasing temperature generally increases rate because particles have more kinetic energy and a greater fraction exceed activation energy. Increasing acid concentration also increases collision frequency; a suitable catalyst can speed some reactions by lowering activation energy.

questions.questionText: For the reversible reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), explain what happens to the equilibrium position when pressure is increased and why. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A school laboratory.
questions.explanation: The system shifts towards the side with fewer gas molecules. There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so increased pressure favours ammonia formation. The change does not alter the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature; it changes the equilibrium composition.

questions.questionText: Describe how a pure, dry sample of copper(II) sulfate crystals could be prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Include the main practical steps. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A small-scale water-treatment investigation.
questions.explanation: Warm dilute sulfuric acid and add copper(II) oxide in small portions while stirring. Continue adding solid until some remains unreacted, showing the acid has been neutralised; filter off excess solid. Concentrate the filtrate by gentle evaporation, allow it to cool to crystallise, then filter and dry the crystals.

questions.questionText: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. Identify the products at the cathode and anode and write half-equations for their formation. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: An industrial chemistry exercise.
questions.explanation: At the cathode, Pb2+ gains electrons: Pb2+ + 2e− → Pb. At the anode, bromide ions lose electrons: 2Br− → Br2 + 2e−. Lead forms at the negative electrode and bromine forms at the positive electrode.

questions.questionText: Explain why iron is extracted in a blast furnace using carbon monoxide and describe the role of limestone in the furnace. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A mining and manufacturing case study.
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide reduces iron(III) oxide to iron because it removes oxygen from the ore. Limestone decomposes on heating to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Calcium oxide reacts with acidic impurities such as silica to form slag, helping separate impurities from molten iron.

questions.questionText: Ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid. State the conditions generally used for this oxidation and explain one practical difference between complete combustion and controlled oxidation. Your work should be presented as a clear, logically ordered response suitable for a ZIMSEC Paper 2 structured question. Context: A household chemistry investigation.
questions.explanation: Ethanol can be oxidised using an oxidising agent such as acidified potassium manganate(VII), with heating; reflux is used when complete oxidation to the acid is required. Complete combustion in excess oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water. Controlled oxidation can form an oxygen-containing organic product such as ethanoic acid rather than fully oxidising all carbon to CO2.

questions.questionText:
Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
(a) Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of CaCO₃ (Ca=40, C=12, O=16). [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the number of moles in 5.0 g of CaCO₃. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at r.t.p. (molar gas volume = 24 dm³). [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Mr(CaCO₃) = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100 [1 mark].
(b) Moles = mass / Mr = 5.0 / 100 = 0.050 mol [2 marks].
(c) 1 mol CaCO₃ produces 1 mol CO₂ -> 0.050 mol CO₂. Volume = 0.050 × 24 = 1.2 dm³ [2 marks].

questions.questionText:
In the Haber process, nitrogen reacts with hydrogen to form ammonia:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)  ΔH = -92 kJ/mol.
(a) State the raw materials from which nitrogen and hydrogen are obtained. [2 marks]
(b) State the industrial conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst) used. [3 marks]
(c) Explain why a very low temperature is not used even though the forward reaction is exothermic. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Nitrogen from fractional distillation of liquid air; hydrogen from natural gas (methane + steam) or electrolysis of water [2 marks].
(b) Temperature ~450°C, pressure ~200 atmospheres, finely divided iron (Fe) catalyst [3 marks].
(c) At very low temperatures the rate of reaction would be far too slow to be economically viable; 450°C is a compromise giving reasonable yield quickly [2 marks].

questions.questionText: Describe the Contact process for the manufacture of sulfuric acid in three main chemical stages, naming the catalyst and giving balanced equations where appropriate. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
Stage 1: Sulfur (or sulfide ore) is burned in air to form sulfur dioxide: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g) [1 mark].
Stage 2: Sulfur dioxide reacts reversibly with oxygen at ~450°C, 1–2 atm, over vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅) catalyst: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) [3 marks].
Stage 3: SO₃ is absorbed into concentrated H₂SO₄ to form oleum (H₂S₂O₇), then safely diluted with water to form concentrated sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) [2 marks].

questions.questionText:
In the blast furnace extraction of iron using haematite (Fe₂O₃), coke (C), and limestone (CaCO₃):
(a) State two functions of coke in the blast furnace. [2 marks]
(b) Write a balanced equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide. [2 marks]
(c) Explain how limestone removes sandy impurities (SiO₂) as slag. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Burns in hot air to supply intense heat (C + O₂ → CO₂) and reacts with CO₂ to produce carbon monoxide reducing agent (CO₂ + C → 2CO) [2 marks].
(b) Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(l) + 3CO₂(g) [2 marks].
(c) Limestone thermally decomposes to CaO (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂); basic CaO reacts with acidic silica: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (molten calcium silicate slag) [2 marks].

questions.questionText:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate (CuSO₄) is electrolysed using inert graphite (carbon) electrodes.
(a) State what is observed at the cathode and write the half-equation. [2 marks]
(b) State what is observed at the anode and write the half-equation. [2 marks]
(c) Explain why the blue colour of the solution gradually fades. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Reddish-brown solid copper deposits on the cathode: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) [2 marks].
(b) Colourless oxygen gas bubbles form at the anode: 4OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) + 4e⁻ [2 marks].
(c) Blue Cu²⁺ ions are continuously removed from solution at the cathode and not replaced by inert carbon electrodes [2 marks].

questions.questionText: Explain, using the collision theory, how increasing (a) temperature [3 marks] and (b) concentration of an acid [3 marks] increases the rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon.
questions.explanation:
(a) Higher temperature increases average kinetic energy of particles, so particles move faster, collide more frequently, and a much higher fraction of collisions exceed activation energy (Ea) [3 marks].
(b) Higher acid concentration means more H⁺ ions per unit volume, causing more frequent successful collisions per second [3 marks].

questions.questionText: Describe step-by-step how to prepare pure dry crystals of zinc sulfate starting from insoluble zinc oxide powder and dilute sulfuric acid. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
1. Warm dilute H₂SO₄ in a beaker and add excess zinc oxide powder while stirring until no more dissolves [2 marks].
2. Filter the mixture to remove unreacted excess zinc oxide residue [1 mark].
3. Gently heat the filtrate to evaporate water until crystallisation point is reached [1 mark].
4. Leave to cool to form crystals, filter, and dry between filter papers [1 mark].

questions.questionText:
Compare Group VII elements (chlorine, bromine, iodine) in terms of:
(a) physical state and colour at room temperature [3 marks],
(b) trend in reactivity down the group and its explanation [3 marks].
questions.explanation:
(a) Chlorine: pale yellow-green gas; Bromine: reddish-brown liquid; Iodine: dark grey-black solid (purple vapour) [3 marks].
(b) Reactivity decreases down Group VII because atomic radius increases and inner shells shield the nucleus, weakening attraction for an incoming outer electron [3 marks].

questions.questionText:
Ethene (C₂H₄) and ethane (C₂H₆) are two hydrocarbons.
(a) State which is unsaturated and give a chemical test to distinguish them, stating the expected observation. [3 marks]
(b) Write the equation for ethene reacting with steam in the presence of phosphoric acid catalyst. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Ethene is unsaturated (contains a C=C double bond). Test: shake each gas with aqueous bromine water. Ethene decolourises orange-brown bromine water rapidly; ethane leaves it orange-brown [3 marks].
(b) C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g) (ethanol) [2 marks].

questions.questionText:
In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution required 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid (HCl) for complete neutralisation.
(a) Write the balanced equation for the reaction. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in mol/dm³. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) [1 mark].
(b) Moles NaOH = (25.0/1000) × 0.10 = 0.0025 mol [1 mark]. Mole ratio 1:1 -> moles HCl = 0.0025 mol [1 mark]. Concentration HCl = 0.0025 / (20.0/1000) = 0.125 mol/dm³ [1 mark].

questions.questionText:
(a) Distinguish between covalent and ionic bonding in terms of electron transfer vs sharing. [2 marks]
(b) Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity whereas molten sodium chloride does. [2 marks]
(c) Explain why simple molecular substances like methane have low melting points. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Ionic bonding involves transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal forming oppositely charged ions; covalent bonding involves sharing pairs of electrons between non-metal atoms [2 marks].
(b) In solid NaCl ions are fixed in a rigid lattice; when molten, ions become mobile and carry charge [2 marks].
(c) Only weak intermolecular forces exist between molecules, needing little heat energy to overcome [2 marks].

questions.questionText: Define temporary and permanent hardness of water, name one ion responsible for water hardness, and give two methods of softening hard water. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Water hardness is caused by dissolved Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺ ions [1 mark]. Temporary hardness (due to hydrogencarbonates) is removed by boiling; permanent hardness (sulfates/chlorides) is not removed by boiling [2 marks]. Softening methods: adding washing soda (Na₂CO₃) to precipitate CaCO₃, or passing through an ion-exchange resin [2 marks].

questions.questionText:
In the fermentation of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) to produce ethanol:
(a) Write the balanced chemical equation. [2 marks]
(b) State why yeast is used and why temperature must be kept around 30–35°C under anaerobic conditions. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g) [2 marks].
(b) Yeast provides enzymes (zymase) that catalyse fermentation [1 mark]. Too hot (>45°C) denatures enzymes; air/oxygen causes ethanoic acid (vinegar) oxidation instead of ethanol [2 marks].

questions.questionText:
Magnesium burns in air and also reacts slowly with steam.
(a) Write balanced equations for magnesium reacting with oxygen and with steam. [2 marks]
(b) Arrange copper, magnesium, zinc, and potassium in decreasing order of reactivity and state how copper is extracted from copper(II) oxide. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂ [2 marks].
(b) Decreasing reactivity: Potassium > Magnesium > Zinc > Copper [2 marks]. Copper is extracted from CuO by heating/reduction with carbon [1 mark].

questions.questionText: Define isotopes using carbon-12 and carbon-14 as examples. Calculate the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in ¹⁴₆C. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same number of protons (atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons (mass numbers) [2 marks]. ¹⁴₆C has 6 protons, 6 electrons, and 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons [2 marks].
